annotations.annotation_text: Page 118 opens Book 1, Chapter 5 ("The Letter from the Midden") during the Age of Gods phase. This passage continues Biddy Doran the Hen scratching up the mysterious letter from the dump, the Book of Kells as model for textual exegesis, featuring The Hen (Biddy Doran), ALP. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.annotation_text: Fall/resurrection motif "wall" on page 118 ("The Letter from the Midden"): Tim Finnegan tumbling from his ladder, Humpty Dumpty shattering from the wall, Adam falling in Eden — all converge within Biddy Doran the Hen scratching up the mysterious letter from the dump, the Book of Kells as model for textual exegesis. The comic-cosmic Fall during the Age of Gods phase demands its counterpart: resurrection through the whiskey-splash of the water of life (uisce beatha).
sources: The Ballad of Tim Finnegan's Wake. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnegan%27s_Wake
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe
Opie, Iona and Peter. The Oxford Dictionary of Nursery Rhymes. https://archive.org/details/oxforddictionary0000unse_m4u1

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 118 ("The Letter from the Midden"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Gods dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
